To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
non‐steroidal, anti‐inflammatory, drug use is associated with an increased risk of developing chronic kidney disease in patients with Type 2 Diabetes.

(i) NSAIDs are associated with an increased risk of CKD in people with T2DM; (ii) this increased risk was observed with both short‐ and long‐term NSAID use; (iii) the association was not modified by the use of ACEIs and/or ARBs.
non‐steroidal drugs are associated with an increased risk of chronic kidney damage in people with diabetes.

NSAIDs should not be used in the treatment of chronic kidney disease, and that they should not be used to treat acute pain in the elderly.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found a significant association of chronic kidney disease with non‐steroidal drug use in people with Type II diabetes.
non‐steroidal, anti‐inflammatory, drugs are associated with increased risk of kidney disease, and that this risk is increased in people with type 2 diabetes mellitius.
the use of NSAIDs is associated with an increased risk of developing CKD in people with T2DM, but that the risk is lower for those taking low doses of aspirin.
The main takeaway from our work is that

NSAID use is associated with an increased risk of CKD, particularly in those who are older, have diabetes and are female, and that this risk is dose dependent, with the highest risk seen with higher doses of NSAID use.
NSAIDs can be used safely in patients with diabetes and CKD, but they should be prescribed at the lowest effective dose, and for the shortest possible duration.
NSAID use is not associated with the development of chronic renal failure in patients with diabetes.
